item.text: I’ll read the five note parts in order, then write the map and run the required check.

item.aggregated_output:
<<55:27 notes, part 0 of 0..4>>
[MUQATIL:55:24-28/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God's face remains; all creatures in the heavens and earth die except God's face, meaning God himself. | mentions 28:88
[MUQATIL:55:24-28/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | When the verse descended, the angels in heaven said the people of earth had perished and wondered how life could benefit them; God's statement in 28:88 assured them all would die. | mentions 28:88
[TAB-FULL:v22p212/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | All jinn and humans on the earth will perish, while God's face remains, possessing majesty and honor.
[TAB-FULL:v22p212/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari parses ذو as an adjective of وجه, explaining its nominative form.
[TAB-FULL:v22p212/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله | reports | Abdullah's reading has ذي in the genitive, making it an adjective of the Lord rather than of the face.
[NAHHAS:v4p308/r3] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | ذو modifies وجه; the intended sense is that your Lord remains, like the expression “the face of the earth.”
[NAHHAS:v4p308/r4] NAHHAS, d. 338 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud reads ذي الجلال والإكرام, making it an adjective of ربك.
[SULAMI:v2p294#3/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | Al-Wasiti says God hides Himself from the elect who witness Him, unlike ordinary people; in this life He gives according to what He discloses inwardly and veils through His wonders, while in the next He gives outwardly and veils through what creatures can bear, hiding Himself only by shielding them from His vision.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Ikram can mean God's honoring His prophets through grace, or servants honoring God through worship and praise for His favors.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r11] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | Hasan and al-Kalbi take ikram as God's honoring the people of His religion and loyalty and His generosity in forgiving His creatures.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r12] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas takes ikram as meaning that none is more honorable, majestic, or great than God.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي ومقاتل | reports | They report that the angels concluded the people of earth had perished when this verse was revealed, then became certain of their own destruction when 28:88 was revealed. | mentions 28:88
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbi says a reader should not pause after the statement that all on earth perish, but continue into the statement that the Lord's face remains.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أهل المعاني | reports | One interpretation takes the Face to mean the Lord's manifestation through His signs, just as a human face makes the person apparent.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أهل المعاني | reports | Another interpretation takes Face as a term for something eminent, so the phrase means the Lord, the exalted Master.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Dhū is an adjective of wajh; if wajh were merely an adjunct of rabbika, the adjective would be dhī rather than nominative dhū.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Jalāl denotes God's greatness and majesty and His right to praised attributes for His beneficence and favor; the word derives from jalla, to be great.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Asmaʿi says jalāl is used only of God.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p158/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو علي | reports | Abu Ali cites poetry in which jalāl describes someone other than God, while allowing that the poem may be pre-Islamic and that al-Asmaʿi meant only God deserves the term after Islam.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:55:19-29/r7] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Wajh here means the Master.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:55:19-29/r8] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | He is possessed of majesty and of honoring His prophets and friends.
[JISHUMI:v9p6714/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · عبد الله | reports | Abdullah reads ذي, making the phrase an adjective of the Lord; the common ذُو is an adjective of وجه.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p445#2/r8] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Dhu al-jalāl describes the Lord as possessing majesty and greatness.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p445#2/r9] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Al-ikrām means that, despite His majesty, God graciously honors His prophets and friends.
[TABRISI:55:24-29/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Arabic idiom uses “face of the opinion” or “face of the plan” for the opinion or plan itself; al-A'sha's poem uses face for the settled judgment.
[TABRISI:55:24-29/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation makes “face” the means by which one draws near to God, supported by a poem pairing God's face with deeds.
[TABRISI:55:24-29/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Death is a favor because it equalizes creatures, leads to reward, warns that worldly life ends, and gives moral agency: immediate reward would compel action and erase its merit.
[TABRISI:55:24-29/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | “The face of your Lord” means the Lord Himself, enduring and manifest through His proofs as a person's face makes him manifest.
[TABRISI:55:24-29/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Majesty denotes greatness, deserving praise, and supreme beneficence, the source of every favor; God honors prophets and friends with His subtle favors.
[TABRISI:55:24-29/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · قيل | reports | Alternatively, God is worthy of reverence and must be declared transcendent from what does not befit His attributes.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p114#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The phrase means that your Lord remains.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p114#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو سليمان الخطابي | reports | Al-Khattabi explains jalal and ikram as verbal nouns: God deserves reverence and honor, and must not be denied or disbelieved.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p114#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Another possible sense is that God honors those devoted to Him and raises their ranks.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p114#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | He also allows one term to describe God’s attribute and the other the servant’s act, as in 74:56: God is worthy of forgiveness and people are to be pious. | mentions 74:56
[RAZI-FULL:v29p120#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Calling the surviving entity ‘the Lord’ might imply He remains as Lord with a subject; saying ‘His face’ removes that implication and asserts the Real’s absolute permanence. | mentions 55:27
[RAZI-FULL:v29p93#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi rejects the corporealist reading of face as an organ: 28:88 says only God's face remains, which would imply that His other bodily parts perish; the sound reading is God's essence, which alone remains. | mentions 28:88
[RAZI-FULL:v29p93#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Against the objection that identifying face with essence erases divine attributes, Razi argues that speech about a remaining garment includes its color and dimensions; likewise God's essence includes His attributes.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p93#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Face is used for a person's whole reality because people say they have seen someone upon seeing the face: its many organs let perception infer more about the person than seeing a hand or foot.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p93#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi rejects the claim in some legal books that face derives from confrontation: the organ-name came first, and related forms were derived from it by later transfer.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p94#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The address most likely reaches every listener: each should attend to God alone, since everything besides Him perishes.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p94#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | He also allows that the address may be directed specifically to Muhammad.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p94#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The singular address includes each hearer while underscoring universal perishability; a dual address could let each addressee exempt himself and his companion.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p94#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Direct address to the Lord signals gentleness while the statement of abiding signals might; the context enumerates kindness and favors.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p94#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rabb is customarily used in an annexed construction; when unannexed, it is paired with another description, as in the cited verses. | mentions 44:8, 1:2, 34:15, 36:58
[RAZI-FULL:v29p94#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Rabb may be a verbal noun meaning upbringing, as in the verbs for raising or nurturing.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p94#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Alternatively, rabb may be an adjective derived from a verbal noun meaning one who nurtures, by analogy with names of agents and qualities.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p94/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | No other divine name works in place of face: known names such as Lord, Creator, and Provider are agent-names, while Allah is sometimes glossed as the worshipped one; calling Him your Lord remaining could suggest a continuing lorded-over object.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p94/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Face of Allah in 2:115 and 30:38 refers to worship: the first passage concerns prayer and the second charity to kin, poor people, and travelers; here, where God's sustaining bounties are discussed, the wording is face of your Lord. | mentions 2:115, 30:38
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | The author says the sounder view is that face means God’s existence and essence, as in idioms meaning the point or essence of a matter.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Other interpretations are that what remains is God made manifest by His proofs, or the direction through which people draw near to
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

 Him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Jalāl means God’s majesty, greatness, and entitlement to attributes of praise; the word derives from jalla, to be great.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Ikram means God deserves reverence and should be declared free of what is unbefitting, such as associating partners with Him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن فورك وأبو المعالي | prefers | The author endorses scholars who take God’s face to mean His existence and essence, which alone remains when creation perishes.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas takes face as a reference to God Himself.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو المعالي | reports | Abu al-Maʿali says most imams understand face as the Creator’s existence; its endurance when creatures perish supports this interpretation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The commentary refers readers to its discussion of 2:115 and fuller treatment in al-Kitāb al-Asnā. | mentions 2:115
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · القشيري | reports | Al-Qushayri reports a view that face is an additional, unqualified attribute through which God turns toward those He chooses to honor.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-28/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي | reports | Anas reports the Prophet urging people to persistently invoke God as Possessor of Majesty and Honor.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-28/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن مسعود | reports | The invocation is also attributed to Ibn Masud and is explained as clinging to that formula in supplication.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-28/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عبيد | reports | Abu Ubayd explains ilẓāẓ as adhering persistently to something, also meaning insistent supplication.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-28/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد المقبري | reports | Saʿid al-Maqburi tells of a man repeatedly invoking God by this name and hearing that his request had been heard.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:55:25-36/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The enduring “face” is God's essence: created things are finite in themselves, except God's face, the aspect facing His direction.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:55:25-36/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | ذو الجلال والإكرام means absolute self-sufficiency and general bounty.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p202#3/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | “The Face of your Lord” means His essence.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p202#3/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Dhu al-jalāl means possessing majesty and sovereignty; it grammatically describes the Face.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p202#3/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Al-ikrām means pardon and beneficence; this is one of God's mighty attributes.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p202#3/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | A hadith urges persistent invocation with the words “O Possessor of Majesty and Honor.”
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p202#3/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet passed a man praying and saying this invocation, and told him that his prayer had been answered.
[QASHANI:55:19-27/r10] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The face that remains after creation’s passing is God’s essence together with all His attributes.
[QASHANI:55:19-27/r11] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Divine majesty is greatness and exaltation: God veils Himself with luminous and dark veils and manifests through dominion and overpowering.
[QASHANI:55:19-27/r12] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Divine generosity is nearness through manifestations of the attributes, and the essence’s appearance through gentleness and mercy.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p61#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Perishing means the extinction of every created thing, while face denotes a thing's reality; God is exempt from bodily limbs. | mentions 28:88
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p61#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The Quraysh poor used face idiomatically to ask where a generous Arab was who would give them aid.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p61#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | Most readers use dhū with wāw as an adjective for wajh; Abū and ʿAbd Allāh read dhī with yāʾ as an adjective for the Lord.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p61#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | The apparent addressee in your Lord's face is the Prophet, which specially honors him; another view makes the address general to every listener.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p61#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Dhu al-jalāl is explained as the one whom monotheists exalt above likeness to creation and their deeds, the one whose majesty inspires awe, or the giver of majesty and honor to sincere servants.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p72/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The ending of worldly blessings with the enduring face matches the end of afterlife blessings with the blessed name: permanence suits the world's passing, while growth suits the increase and duration of Paradise's gifts.
[SAMIN-DURR:55:27/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The common reading has ذو nominative as an adjective of وجه; Ubayy and Abd Allah read ذي genitive as an adjective of ربك.
[SAMIN-DURR:55:27/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Al-Samin notes that the seven readers differ again on this phrase at the end of the sura.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p494/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says God first informed people about what He created, then informed them that all of it would pass away.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p494/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | reports | Ibn Kathir cites a transmitted supplication calling God the Ever-Living, Self-Subsisting, Creator of the heavens and earth, and the Possessor of Majesty and Honor, asking for mercy, rectitude, and protection from reliance on self or creation.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p494/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbi says one should not stop after reciting that all on earth perish, but continue through the declaration that God's Face remains.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p494/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The verse parallels 28:88, that everything perishes except God's Face, and connects seeking God's Face with worship and charity in 18:28 and 76:9. | mentions 28:88, 18:28, 76:9
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p494/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | God's Face is characterized by Majesty and Honor: God is worthy to be revered without disobedience and obeyed without defiance.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p494/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses Possessor of Majesty and Honor as Possessor of greatness and pride.
[BURHAN:v2p51/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The permanence of the Lord’s face does not conflict with the statement that all on earth perish.
[NASHR:v1p224#2/r6] NASHR, d. 833 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbī says not to pause after kullu man ʿalayhā fān until reciting wa-yabqā wajhu rabbika dhu al-jalāli wa-l-ikrām. | mentions 55:27
[NASHR:v2p382/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | All readers use wāw in the first occurrence, wa-yabqā wajhu rabbika dhu al-jalāl; it modifies wajh and cannot be an insertion, as all codices agree.
[NASHR:v2p63#2/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · author | reports | Ibn Dhakwan differs in reports on imāla for عمران, الإكرام, and إكراههن; the Tajrid records only imāla, through al-Akhfash and several transmitters. | mentions 3:36, 24:33, 55:27
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p385/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The face is the noblest part of a being and can stand for its possessor; since it cannot remain apart from its possessor, it conveys the continued existence of the whole after creation perishes.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p385/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | God remains forever after all else perishes. ‘Your Lord’s face’ refers to his essence, the noblest aspect of his being; the wording is more eloquent than ‘its possessor.’
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p385/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Lord is the one who nurtures the Prophet through the message and revelation toward boundless knowledge; seeking his face also means acting sincerely for God.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p385/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The religious principle that nothing resembles God prevents a corporeal reading of ‘face’; God is free of need and deficiency, unlike all observable creatures.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p385/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | ‘Possessor of majesty’ describes God’s essence: unsurpassable greatness that excludes everything unworthy of him.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p385/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | ‘And honor’ describes God’s action, his general beneficence.
[DURR-FULL:v7p698/r3] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbī advises readers not to stop after the statement that all on earth perish, but to continue through the statement that God's face remains.
[DURR-FULL:v7p698/r4] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses ذو الجلال والإكرام as possessing majesty and greatness.
[DURR-FULL:v7p698/r5] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · رجل | reports | A man prayed for God's sufficient, generous face; al-Bayhaqī's wording instead calls it the abiding, beautiful face.
[ITQAN:v1p222/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbi says not to pause after 55:26 but to continue reading through 55:27; Suyuti says Ibn Abi Hatim recorded this.
[ITQAN:v2p332#2/r9] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Dhu al-jalal means possessing majesty and greatness.
[ITQAN:v3p13/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · جمهور أهل السنة | reports | The majority of Sunnis, including the early authorities and hadith scholars, affirm the attribute verses, consign their intended meaning to God, and deny that their literal realities apply to Him. | mentions 20:5, 28:88, 20:39, 48:10, 39:67
[ITQAN:v3p13/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · محمد بن الحسن | reports | Muhammad ibn al-Hasan says the jurists unanimously affirmed the divine attributes without interpretation or likening God to creation. | mentions 20:5, 28:88, 20:39
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

, 48:10, 39:67
[ITQAN:v3p13/r7] ITQAN, d. 911 · سفيان الثوري ومالك وابن المبارك وابن عيينة ووكيع | reports | Al-Tirmidhi says these leading imams transmit the reports as received and believe them, without asking how, interpreting, or imagining their modality. | mentions 20:5, 28:88, 20:39, 48:10, 39:67
[ITQAN:v3p13/r8] ITQAN, d. 911 · طائفة من أهل السنة | reports | A later Sunni group interprets the attribute verses in a way fitting God’s majesty; this is the position of the later scholars. | mentions 20:5, 28:88, 20:39, 48:10, 39:67
[ITQAN:v3p13/r9] ITQAN, d. 911 · إمام الحرمين | prefers | Al-Juwayni first held figurative interpretation, then recanted and said the doctrine he accepted was to follow the early Muslims, who left the meanings unprobed. | mentions 20:5, 28:88, 20:39, 48:10, 39:67
[ITQAN:v3p17/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid treats the hand as an emphatic addition like “the Face of your Lord”; al-Baghawi rejects this as weak, since it would erase Adam’s distinction from Satan. | mentions 38:75, 55:27
[ITQAN:v3p236/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Iftinān joins two modes, praise and consolation: God comforts all creatures capable of life by announcing their end, then praises His own abiding majesty and generosity in ten words.
[ITQAN:v3p98/r4] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The reverse figure names a part for the whole: 'face' means God's essence or the person facing, body-wide states are expressed by faces or hands, and prayer's standing, reciting, bowing, or prostrating can stand for the whole prayer. | mentions 55:27, 2:144, 88:8, 88:3, 2:286, 2:184, 17:78, 76:26, 2:43, 5:95
[BURSEVI:v9p243/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن الشيخ | reports | Ibn al-Shaykh says 'face' may mean direction, since no direction lacks a face toward which one turns; he connects this to the expression 'in God's side.' | mentions 39:56
[BURSEVI:v9p243/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن الشيخ | reports | Ibn al-Shaykh adds that earthly beings and their works perish except what they direct toward God and do in pursuit of His good pleasure.
[BURSEVI:v9p243/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الملائكة | reports | The angels first thought the children of Adam had perished when this verse was revealed; after 'every soul tastes death' was revealed, they realized they too would die, since their subtle bodies and attached spirits perish, though the lofty, immaterial spirits do not. | mentions 3:185
[BURSEVI:v9p243/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The 'face' of the Lord means His essence; face, the noblest bodily member and locus of the senses, is borrowed as an expression for the essence.
[BURSEVI:v9p243/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · القاضي | reports | Al-Qadi says that examining the aspects of all existing things shows them to be perishing in themselves, except for the face of God turned toward His direction.
[BURSEVI:v9p243/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · سعدي المفتي | reports | Saʿdi al-Mufti suggests that 'face' can mean aim or intention, and that the phrase about directions is loosely worded, with the genitive explaining the aim toward which one turns.
[BURSEVI:v9p244/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Dhu al-Jalal wa-al-Ikram describes God as absolutely self-sufficient or majestic in essence and attributes, and as possessing complete generosity.
[BURSEVI:v9p244/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعضهم | reports | Some say that deeper discernment reveals the actual perishing of the universe even while it appears to exist, since what depends on another is not truly self-subsisting; real existence belongs to the pre-eternal.
[BURSEVI:v9p244/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | The Prophet urges people to persist in invoking God by the name 'Possessor of Majesty and Generosity.'
[BURSEVI:v9p244/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | The Prophet passed a man praying with this invocation and told him his supplication had been answered, so calling on God by these two names is likely to be accepted.
